title: Core memory and the transistorized computers
text:
CHAPTER 5. THE TRANSISTOR
SECTION 5.4. CORE MEMORY AND THE TRANSISTORIZED COMPUTERS

The transistor solved the switching problem, but a computer is only as good as its memory. Delay lines were serial and temperamental, Williams tubes needed constant adjustment, and magnetic drums were slow. In the early 1950s a new technology, magnetic-core memory, gave computers fast, reliable, random-access storage that did not forget when the power went off. Core memory plus transistor logic defined the second generation of computers, from the mid-1950s to the late 1960s. These were the machines on which artificial intelligence research began: the first AI programs ran on IBM's 704 and its transistorized successors, and the MIT hacker culture that shaped AI labs grew up around the TX-0 and PDP-1.

1. Magnetic hysteresis as memory

A small ring ("core") of ferrite, a ceramic magnetic material, can be magnetized clockwise or counterclockwise around its circumference. These two directions of magnetization are the two states of a bit.

The material has a nearly square hysteresis loop. Plot the magnetic flux density B in the core against the magnetizing field H, which is proportional to the current through wires passing through the ring:

  - Below a threshold field Hc, the core's magnetization barely changes, whichever state it is in.
  - Above +Hc, the core switches to the "1" direction; below -Hc, to the "0" direction.
  - When the current is removed, the core stays in the last state: it is non-volatile.

So a core is a one-bit memory element that holds its state with no power at all, and switches only when driven past a threshold. That threshold is what makes large arrays possible.

2. Coincident-current addressing

Arrange cores in a grid, like beads on a mesh of wires. Each core has an X wire and a Y wire passing through it. To write to the core at (row i, column j):

  - Send current I/2 along X wire i and I/2 along Y wire j, where I is just enough to switch a core.
  - The one core at the intersection receives I/2 + I/2 = I and switches.
  - Every other core on wire i or wire j receives only I/2, below threshold, and is unaffected.

This is the coincident-current scheme. Its key patent went to Jay Forrester at MIT, who developed it for the Whirlwind computer. Other researchers in the late 1940s and early 1950s also conceived core memories, including An Wang and Way-Dong Woo at Harvard (a "pulse transfer controlling device," 1949, patented by Wang) and Jan Rajchman at RCA; the resulting patent disputes were eventually settled.

Reading is destructive. To read a core, the memory drives it toward "0." A third wire, the sense wire, threads through every core in the plane. If the core was "1," it flips and its changing flux induces a voltage pulse on the sense wire; if it was already "0," there is only a small noise pulse. So the read tells you the bit but leaves the core at 0. The memory controller therefore immediately writes the bit back. A full read cycle is read-then-restore. (An inhibit wire, carrying a current that cancels half the write current, is used during the restore to leave a core at 0 when needed.)

A 3D core stack has one plane per bit of the word, all planes addressed together, so a whole word is read or written at once.

Speed and capacity. Early core memories in the mid-1950s had cycle times of perhaps 10 to 20 microseconds; by the late 1960s cycle times under 1 microsecond were common. Capacities grew from a few thousand words to around a million. Cores were strung by hand, often by women workers with fine needles under magnifiers, which made core memory labor intensive; manufacturing moved largely to Asia to reduce cost.

Whirlwind, MIT's real-time computer for air defense research, received core memory in 1953, replacing its unreliable electrostatic storage tubes and greatly improving its speed and reliability. Core memory then spread across the industry. It was used in the IBM 704 (announced in 1954, a vacuum tube machine with core memory), in the SAGE air defense system, and in essentially all second-generation computers.

Legacy. Core remained the standard main memory until semiconductor DRAM displaced it in the 1970s (Intel's 1103 DRAM chip, 1970, is usually cited as the turning point). Its names survive: a "core dump" is still the term for a snapshot of a program's memory. Core memory was also extremely robust, which is why the Apollo Guidance Computer used it, together with "core rope" read-only memory, where software was literally woven: a wire threaded through a core meant 1, a wire bypassing it meant 0.

3. The first transistor computers

Several groups competed to build computers from transistors in the early-to-mid 1950s:

  - The University of Manchester's experimental Transistor Computer was first operational in November 1953, widely regarded as the first transistor computer to operate anywhere. The prototype used 92 point-contact transistors and 550 diodes. A full-size version followed in April 1955, with 200 point-contact transistors and 1,300 diodes and a power consumption of 150 W. It still used some vacuum tubes in its clock generator, and the early point-contact transistors were unreliable. A production version, the Metrovick 950, was built in small numbers.
  - Bell Labs' TRADIC (completed January 1954), built for the US Air Force, used transistors and diodes for its logic but a vacuum tube amplifier to supply its 1 MHz clock power.
  - The Harwell CADET in Britain, first operating in February 1955, is one of the candidates for first fully transistorized computer, though it ran at a slow 58 kHz.
  - MIT Lincoln Laboratory's TX-0, operational in 1956, was built as a test machine for transistor circuits and a large core memory. It used Philco surface-barrier transistors.

By the end of the 1950s the major manufacturers were shipping transistorized machines in volume.

4. The second generation in industry

  IBM 7090 (first installed December 1959). A transistorized version of IBM's tube-based 709 scientific computer, roughly five or six times faster, used for scientific computing, aerospace work and military systems; the US Air Force used 7090s in the Ballistic Missile Early Warning System (BMEWS) for decades. The 7090 and its successor 7094 were workhorses of 1960s research computing, including AI research at MIT, Stanford and elsewhere.

  IBM 1401 (announced October 5, 1959). A transistorized business computer that worked in variable-length decimal, used for accounting and data processing. More than 12,000 units were produced, making it one of the most successful computers of its era and bringing electronic computing to many medium-sized businesses for the first time. It typically rented rather than sold, with monthly rental starting at about $2,500.

  DEC PDP-1 (first produced 1959). Digital Equipment Corporation, founded in 1957 by Ken Olsen and Harlan Anderson, who came from MIT Lincoln Lab's TX-0 and TX-2 projects, built the PDP-1 as a relatively inexpensive, interactive computer with a CRT display. It is regarded as a precursor of the minicomputer. MIT received one in 1961, and students there wrote Spacewar!, one of the earliest digital video games, on it in 1962.

  IBM System/360 (announced April 7, 1964). Strictly a hybrid between the second and third generations: it used IBM's Solid Logic Technology, small modules with discrete transistor and diode chips mounted on ceramic substrates, rather than true integrated circuits. Its great innovation was architectural: a whole family of compatible computers, from small to large, sharing one instruction set, so customers could upgrade without rewriting software. It standardized the 8-bit byte, and most models implemented their instruction set using microcode (Wilkes's idea from Section 4.4). Its success made IBM dominant in computing for two decades.

5. Software in the second generation

Transistors and core memory made computers reliable and fast enough that software, not hardware, became the main challenge.

  - High-level languages. FORTRAN (IBM, John Backus's team, first delivered in 1957 for the IBM 704) made scientific programming far easier and showed that compiled code could be nearly as efficient as hand-written assembly. COBOL (1959-1960) followed for business. LISP (John McCarthy, from 1958, first implemented on the IBM 704) became the language of AI (Section 9.2).
  - Operating systems and batch processing. Machines were expensive, so jobs were queued and run in batches by operators, with programmers submitting decks of punched cards and waiting hours for printouts.
  - Time-sharing. To let many people use one computer interactively, researchers developed time-sharing systems in which the computer switches rapidly between users. MIT's Compatible Time-Sharing System (CTSS), demonstrated in 1961 on an IBM 709 and later run on a 7090/7094, was an early example. John McCarthy was among the early advocates of time-sharing, partly because interactive computing suited AI programming. Project MAC, founded at MIT in 1963, combined time-sharing research with the AI group led by Marvin Minsky and McCarthy's former colleagues.

6. The hacker culture and AI

The TX-0 (loaned to MIT's campus from Lincoln Lab in the late 1950s) and the PDP-1 were unusual in that individual users could sit at the console and interact with the machine directly, watching results on a screen and changing programs immediately. A culture of student programmers, later chronicled as the original "hackers" (in the sense of skilled, playful programmers), formed around these machines and the Tech Model Railroad Club at MIT. Many of them became the programmers of the MIT AI Lab, writing early LISP systems, debugging tools, text editors, chess programs and the Incompatible Timesharing System (ITS).

The point for this book: AI research has always depended on the computers available. Symbolic AI of the 1960s was made possible by transistorized, core-memory computers with interactive time-sharing; its ambitions were limited by memory sizes measured in tens or hundreds of thousands of words. Neural network research, by contrast, needed far more arithmetic than these machines could supply, a constraint that would only be lifted decades later.

7. Comparing memory technologies, 1945-1970

    Technology          Access        Typical cycle     Volatile?   Notes
    ----------          ------        -------------     ---------   -----
    Mercury delay line  serial        ~100s of us avg   yes         temperature sensitive
    Williams tube       random        ~10 us            yes         needs refresh and tuning
    Magnetic drum       serial (rot.) ~ms               no          cheap, large, slow
    Magnetic core       random        ~10 us to <1 us   no          reliable, hand-assembled
    Semiconductor DRAM  random        <1 us (1970)      yes         needs refresh; dense, cheap

The progression shows two engineering forces that still operate: the drive toward random access with uniform latency, and the drive toward density and cost per bit, which eventually favored semiconductor memory made by the same photolithographic processes as logic (Chapter 6).

8. Why the transistor era mattered for AI

  - Reliability: transistorized machines ran for long periods without failure, so researchers could run long, complex programs, such as search-based game players and theorem provers.
  - Availability: universities could afford and maintain them, so AI research could begin in academic labs (Dartmouth, MIT, Carnegie Tech, Stanford).
  - Interactivity: time-sharing and display consoles allowed the exploratory style of programming that AI researchers favored.
  - Limits: memory of perhaps 32K to 256K words and speeds of hundreds of thousands of instructions per second meant AI programs had to be clever, compact and symbolic. Learning from large data was out of reach.

9. Summary

  - Magnetic cores store bits as the direction of magnetization in ferrite rings with square hysteresis loops; coincident-current addressing (Forrester; also Wang, Woo, Rajchman) selects one core with half-currents on X and Y wires.
  - Reads are destructive and followed by rewrite; core memory was non-volatile, random access and reliable, and it was the standard main memory from the mid-1950s until DRAM displaced it in the 1970s.
  - Early transistor computers included Manchester's Transistor Computer (November 1953), Bell Labs' TRADIC (January 1954), the Harwell CADET (February 1955) and MIT Lincoln Lab's TX-0 (1956).
  - Second-generation machines included the IBM 7090 (December 1959), the IBM 1401 (announced October 1959, over 12,000 built) and DEC's PDP-1 (1959); the IBM System/360 (announced April 7, 1964) introduced a compatible family architecture.
  - FORTRAN, LISP and time-sharing flourished on these machines, and MIT's interactive computing culture fed directly into AI research.
